Foods with a hole in the middle.Bagel: Bagels are boiled briefly before baking, which gives their chewy crust, and the hole makes them easy to string or stack.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Doughnut: The doughnut hole is credited to an American ship captain, Hanson Gregory, who in 1847 said he punched out the center.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Cheerios: Cheerios started in 1941 as Cheeri Oats, and the ring shape comes from a puffing machine.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Polo mint: Polo mints are British, and the hole in their middle gave rise to the slogan 'the mint with the hole'.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Life Savers: Life Savers were created in 1912 by chocolatier Clarence Crane as a summer candy, shaped like lifebuoys.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Onion ring: Onion rings are battered slices of onion, and the hole is simply where the middle layers were removed.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Pineapple ring: Pineapple rings come from coring the fruit, and a machine invented by Henry Ginaca in 1911 sped up canning.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Froot Loops: Froot Loops are ring-shaped cereal, and the loop is a hole; toucan Sam's loops come in several colors that share one flavor.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Calamari: Calamari rings are cut from the body tube of a squid, giving them the hole in the middle.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Bundt cake: The bundt pan, from a German Bundkuchen, has a central tube so that dense batter bakes evenly.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Muffin: Muffins are baked in cups, with no hole, and the American kind is sweeter and bigger than the English kind.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Croissant: Croissants are crescent-shaped, flaky pastries, and legend ties them to Vienna, though the modern version is French.
Foods with a hole in the middle.English muffin: English muffins are cooked on a griddle, and their nooks and crannies are no hole, perfect for catching butter.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Pancake: Pancakes are flat griddle cakes, and they have no hole, and in many countries have a day, Shrove Tuesday.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Biscuit: A biscuit is a southern American quick bread, and is solid, with no hole, unlike the British biscuit, which is a cookie.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Scone: Scones are British baked treats served with cream and jam, and are solid.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Brownie: Brownies are dense chocolate squares, and are solid, which are said to have been invented by accident.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Pizza: Pizza has no hole; its Neapolitan style is UNESCO-listed, with a soft, thin crust baked in a wood-fired oven in around a minute.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Madeleine: Madeleines are shell-shaped French sponge cakes, famously triggering memories in Proust's novel.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Macaron: Macarons are filled almond meringue sandwiches, and are solid, which are not to be confused with coconut macaroons.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Pita: Pita puffs up in a hot oven to make a pocket, but the pocket isn't a hole through the middle.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Bialy: The bialy looks like a bagel and has a depression in the middle that is not a hole, but filled with onion.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Jelly doughnut: A jelly doughnut has filling in place of a hole, so it has no hole through its middle.
Foods with a hole in the middle.Cupcake: Cupcakes are small cakes baked in paper cups, and have no hole, and the name may come from the cups used for measuring.

Caribbean dishes.Jerk chicken: Jamaican jerk gets its heat from Scotch bonnet peppers and its aroma from allspice (pimento) wood, a method traced to the Maroons.
Caribbean dishes.Ackee and saltfish: Jamaica's national dish uses ackee, a fruit that's toxic until it ripens and opens on the tree, and it scrambles like eggs.
Caribbean dishes.Doubles: Trinidad's favorite street breakfast tucks curried chickpeas between two fried flatbreads called bara.
Caribbean dishes.Callaloo: A hearty green stew of dasheen leaves or amaranth with coconut milk, popular in Trinidad and Tobago and across the islands.
Caribbean dishes.Mofongo: Puerto Rican fried green plantains mashed with garlic and pork cracklings, a dish with West African roots.
Caribbean dishes.Rice and peas: The 'peas' are actually kidney beans, and the rice is cooked in coconut milk; it's a Jamaican Sunday dinner staple.
Caribbean dishes.Conch fritters: Crispy balls of chopped conch, a sea snail, are a Bahamian specialty, and the shell is a common souvenir.
Caribbean dishes.Jamaican patty: This turmeric-tinted pastry stuffed with spiced beef was inspired by Cornish pasties and Indian curry spices, and is sold across Jamaica.
Caribbean dishes.Ropa vieja: Cuba's national dish, shredded beef in tomato sauce, means 'old clothes' in Spanish after the stringy look of the meat.
Caribbean dishes.Pastelón: A Puerto Rican and Dominican sweet-plantain 'lasagna' layered with seasoned ground beef and cheese.
Caribbean dishes.Gumbo: This one belongs to Louisiana, with French, Spanish and West African influences, rather than the Caribbean.
Caribbean dishes.Jambalaya: Louisiana's rice dish is a cousin of Spanish paella and doesn't count as Caribbean.
Caribbean dishes.Feijoada: Brazilian black bean and pork stew, so it is South American, not Caribbean.
Caribbean dishes.Tamales: Corn dough steamed in husks goes back thousands of years in Mesoamerica; it's Mexican and Central American.
Caribbean dishes.Pupusa: El Salvador's stuffed tortilla is Central American, not Caribbean.
Caribbean dishes.Poke: Hawaii's marinated raw fish salad comes from the Pacific, not the Caribbean; the word means 'to slice' in Hawaiian.
Caribbean dishes.Pad thai: Thailand's noodle stir-fry is Southeast Asian, not Caribbean.
Caribbean dishes.Chili con carne: The spicy beef stew is a Texas classic, though Mexico never really claims it.
Caribbean dishes.Moussaka: Greece's baked eggplant and meat dish has nothing Caribbean about it.
Caribbean dishes.Biltong: Dried meat from South Africa, brought by Dutch settlers; it's African, not Caribbean.
Caribbean dishes.Poutine: Fries with cheese curds and gravy are a Quebec invention from the 1950s, a Canadian comfort food rather than a Caribbean one.
Caribbean dishes.Shepherd's pie: A British dish of minced lamb under mashed potato; with beef it's technically cottage pie.
Caribbean dishes.Paella: Spain's rice dish isn't Caribbean, though Spanish rule left its mark on dishes like Cuban arroz con pollo.
Caribbean dishes.Haggis: Scotland's famous savory pudding of sheep offal, oats and spices, is eaten on Burns Night and isn't Caribbean in any way.

Parts of a flower.Petal: Petals are modified leaves that attract pollinators. Some flowers, like bee orchids, use petal shapes that mimic insects.
Parts of a flower.Sepal: Sepals are the green, leaf-like parts that wrap a bud. In tulips and lilies they look like petals, and the pair are called tepals.
Parts of a flower.Stamen: The stamen is the male part, a stalk topped by an anther. A flower's stamens may number from a few to several hundred.
Parts of a flower.Pistil: The pistil is the female part, made of stigma, style and ovary. Some flowers have a single pistil, others several fused.
Parts of a flower.Anther: The anther is the pollen-making tip of the stamen. In some flowers, such as tomato, it releases pollen only when vibrated by a buzzing bee.
Parts of a flower.Stigma: The stigma is the sticky tip that catches pollen. Pollen grains grow a tube down through the style to reach the ovules.
Parts of a flower.Style: The style is the slender stalk linking stigma to ovary. In corn, the long silk threads are styles, each leading to one kernel.
Parts of a flower.Ovary: The ovary holds the ovules and ripens into the fruit. That is why a tomato or a pea pod is botanically a fruit.
Parts of a flower.Filament: The filament is the thin stalk that holds the anther up. Its job is to place pollen where visitors will brush against it.
Parts of a flower.Pollen: Pollen grains carry the plant's male cells, and each species has a distinctive shape. This lets scientists identify ancient climates from fossil pollen.
Parts of a flower.Receptacle: The receptacle is the base of the flower where parts attach. In strawberries, the red flesh is a swollen receptacle, and the 'seeds' are the real fruits.
Parts of a flower.Nectary: The nectary produces sweet nectar to lure pollinators. Some flowers hide it deep in a spur, so only long-tongued visitors can reach it.
Parts of a flower.Bark: Bark is on woody stems and trunks, not flowers. In the cork oak it's harvested every nine years or so without killing the tree.
Parts of a flower.Root: Roots anchor a plant and absorb water, not part of the flower. Some trees have roots that spread much wider than the crown.
Parts of a flower.Trunk: A trunk is a tree's main stem. The oldest known individual trees are over 4,000 years old, such as bristlecone pines.
Parts of a flower.Twig: A twig is a small woody shoot. Its buds hold next year's leaves and flowers, which are formed the summer before.
Parts of a flower.Cone: Cones are the seed-bearing structures of conifers, not flowers. Pines have male and female cones separate on the same tree.
Parts of a flower.Spore: Spores are how ferns, mosses and fungi reproduce, with no flower involved. One puffball can release trillions of them.
Parts of a flower.Frond: A frond is a fern's leaf, which uncurls from a coil called a fiddlehead. Ferns don't flower at all, and reproduce by spores.
Parts of a flower.Bulb: A bulb is an underground storage organ. Onions and tulips are bulbs, but bulbs are not parts of a flower.
Parts of a flower.Tuber: A tuber, like a potato, is a swollen underground stem. The 'eyes' on a potato are buds that can sprout new plants.
Parts of a flower.Thorn: A thorn is a modified stem or branch, as on hawthorn. It's different from a prickle on roses, which grows from the skin.
Parts of a flower.Needle: A needle is the leaf of a conifer. Its waxy coating and narrow shape cut water loss in winter.
Parts of a flower.Rhizome: A rhizome is a creeping underground stem. Ginger and bamboo spread this way, and some bamboo forests are single connected plants.

Foods named after people.Beef Stroganoff: Beef Stroganoff takes its name from the noble Russian Stroganov family, long associated with fine dining and wealth.
Foods named after people.Graham cracker: Graham crackers come from the minister Sylvester Graham, who preached eating whole wheat in the 1800s as a way to curb passions.
Foods named after people.Oysters Rockefeller: Oysters Rockefeller was created at Antoine's in New Orleans in 1899 and named for John D. Rockefeller because the sauce was so rich.
Foods named after people.Bananas Foster: Bananas Foster was invented in 1951 at Brennan's in New Orleans and named for Richard Foster, a friend of the owner.
Foods named after people.Chicken Tetrazzini: Chicken Tetrazzini honors the Italian opera soprano Luisa Tetrazzini, and the creamy pasta bake is thought to have been made for her in San Francisco.
Foods named after people.Eggs Benedict: Eggs Benedict may be named for Lemuel Benedict, who ordered it in 1894 at the Waldorf in New York, but other origin stories compete.
Foods named after people.Peach Melba: Peach Melba was devised by chef Auguste Escoffier for the soprano Nellie Melba, whose stage name came from her hometown, Melbourne.
Foods named after people.Pavlova: Pavlova is named for the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, supposedly because the dessert is as light as her tutu.
Foods named after people.Nachos: Nachos were invented by Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya in Mexico in 1943, and the dish is simply his nickname.
Foods named after people.Carpaccio: Carpaccio is named after the Renaissance painter Vittore Carpaccio, who used strong reds that reminded the inventor of raw beef.
Foods named after people.Earl Grey: Earl Grey is likely named for Charles, 2nd Earl Grey, a British prime minister in the 1830s, though the origin story is murky.
Foods named after people.Cobb salad: Cobb salad is named for Robert Cobb, the Brown Derby restaurant owner, who reportedly assembled it from leftovers in the kitchen.
Foods named after people.Brie: Brie is named after the Brie region of France near Paris, so it's a place name, not a person.
Foods named after people.Roquefort: Roquefort comes from the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in France, and it's aged in natural limestone caves.
Foods named after people.Cognac: Cognac is named for the town of Cognac in France, and only brandy from that area may bear the name.
Foods named after people.Lima bean: Lima beans are named after Lima, Peru, so they're a place name and not tied to anyone.
Foods named after people.Bourbon: Bourbon is named for Bourbon County, Kentucky, which was itself named for France's royal House of Bourbon.
Foods named after people.Port wine: Port wine is named for Porto in Portugal, from which it was shipped, and it's fortified with brandy.
Foods named after people.Neapolitan: Neapolitan ice cream and pizza are named for Naples, so they're place names, not honors to a person.
Foods named after people.Chicken Kiev: Chicken Kiev is named for the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, so it's named for a place, though its origin may lie elsewhere.
Foods named after people.Gruyère: Gruyère is named for the Swiss town of Gruyères, so it's named for a place, not a person.
Foods named after people.Mocha: Mocha comes from the Yemeni port of Mocha, which was once a major coffee trading hub.
Foods named after people.Parmesan: Parmesan means from Parma, an Italian city, so it's named for a place and not a person.
Foods named after people.Bologna: Bologna takes its name from the Italian city of Bologna, so it's a place, not a person.

Ten largest countries by area.Russia: The largest country by far, covering about 17 million square km, or one eighth of Earth's land. It spans 11 time zones.
Ten largest countries by area.Canada: The second largest country has the longest coastline in the world and more lakes than the rest of the world combined. Its population is smaller than California's.
Ten largest countries by area.USA: Its area ranks third or fourth, with China, depending on how you count. It has about 9.8 million square km.
Ten largest countries by area.China: It ranks third or fourth in area, about 9.6 million square km, but all of it officially uses a single time zone.
Ten largest countries by area.Brazil: The fifth largest country covers nearly half of South America. It borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
Ten largest countries by area.Australia: Sixth largest by area, and the only country that's an entire continent. It is about the same size as the lower 48 US states.
Ten largest countries by area.India: The seventh largest country by area, at about 3.3 million square km, is also the most populous.
Ten largest countries by area.Argentina: Eighth largest country at about 2.8 million square km. It stretches from the tropics to near Antarctica.
Ten largest countries by area.Kazakhstan: The biggest landlocked country, ninth overall, at about 2.7 million square km. Most of its land is steppe, and it hosts the Baikonur cosmodrome.
Ten largest countries by area.Algeria: Africa's largest country since Sudan split in 2011 and the tenth in the world, about 2.4 million square km, with most of it in the Sahara.
Ten largest countries by area.Mexico: Mexico ranks around 13th, at about 1.96 million square km, so it just misses the top ten.
Ten largest countries by area.Greenland: The world's largest island has an area of about 2.2 million square km, which would rank it 12th, but it's a territory of Denmark and not a sovereign country.
Ten largest countries by area.DR Congo: The second largest country in Africa, at about 2.3 million square km, ranks 11th in the world, just missing the top ten.
Ten largest countries by area.Saudi Arabia: It ranks around 12th by area, at about 2.15 million square km, so it's outside the top ten.
Ten largest countries by area.Indonesia: Indonesia is about 1.9 million square km, which is about 14th, though it has the world's most islands in one country.
Ten largest countries by area.Iran: Ranks about 17th, at about 1.65 million square km, so it's outside the top ten.
Ten largest countries by area.Mongolia: Roughly 1.56 million square km, ranking about 18th. It's large but also the least densely populated sovereign country.
Ten largest countries by area.Libya: Libya ranks around 16th at about 1.76 million square km. Most of it is desert.
Ten largest countries by area.Sudan: Sudan fell out of the top ten when South Sudan split off in 2011, and is now about 1.86 million square km.
Ten largest countries by area.Peru: Peru covers about 1.28 million square km, ranking around 19th.
Ten largest countries by area.Chad: Chad covers about 1.28 million square km, ranking about 20th.
Ten largest countries by area.Egypt: Egypt covers about 1 million square km, though most people live in a thin strip along the Nile.
Ten largest countries by area.Nigeria: Nigeria covers about 924,000 square km, so it's far smaller than the top ten, though it is Africa's most populous country.
Ten largest countries by area.South Africa: South Africa covers about 1.22 million square km, ranking about 24th.

Places in Scotland.Loch Ness: The lake holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined, and sightings of its monster date back to 565 AD.
Places in Scotland.Ben Nevis: At 1,345 meters, the highest mountain in the British Isles, and a strange sight, as an old observatory once stood on its summit.
Places in Scotland.Edinburgh Castle: Perched on an extinct volcano, it holds the Scottish crown jewels, and a one o'clock gun fires every day but Sunday.
Places in Scotland.Isle of Skye: The largest of the Inner Hebrides, with the jagged Cuillin range and the strange rock pinnacles of the Old Man of Storr.
Places in Scotland.Glencoe: A dramatic glen, and scene of the 1692 massacre of the MacDonalds, and a filming spot for Skyfall.
Places in Scotland.Arthur's Seat: An extinct volcano rising 250 meters above Edinburgh, which anyone can climb in under an hour.
Places in Scotland.Cairngorms: The UK's largest national park, with the highest plateau in the country and reindeer herd roaming wild.
Places in Scotland.Orkney: Islands north of mainland Scotland, with Skara Brae, a Stone Age village older than Stonehenge and the pyramids.
Places in Scotland.Shetland: The islands lie closer to Norway than to Edinburgh, and are famous for their small ponies and wool.
Places in Scotland.Loch Lomond: The largest lake in Britain by surface area, immortalized in the song about its bonnie banks.
Places in Scotland.St Andrews: The home of golf, whose Old Course dates to the 15th century, and where Prince William studied.
Places in Scotland.Snowdonia: A Welsh national park, home to Wales's highest peak, Snowdon, so it is not Scottish.
Places in Scotland.Lake District: England's lake region, home of poet William Wordsworth, not Scotland.
Places in Scotland.Giant's Causeway: A Northern Irish coast of 40,000 basalt columns formed by lava, tied to the legend of the giant Finn McCool.
Places in Scotland.Stonehenge: The Wiltshire stone circle in England, about 5,000 years old, with some stones brought from Wales.
Places in Scotland.Hadrian's Wall: The Roman wall across northern England, not Scotland, about 73 miles long, begun in 122 AD.
Places in Scotland.Lindisfarne: An English tidal island and a Viking raid site in 793, which began the Viking Age.
Places in Scotland.Isle of Man: A self-governing island in the Irish Sea, with its own parliament and the famous TT motorcycle races.
Places in Scotland.Cliffs of Moher: Spectacular Irish sea cliffs on the Atlantic coast of County Clare, rising up to about 214 meters.
Places in Scotland.Dartmoor: A wild moor in Devon, England, with free-roaming ponies, which inspired the Hound of the Baskervilles.
Places in Scotland.Yorkshire Dales: An English national park of limestone valleys and the home of Wensleydale cheese.
Places in Scotland.Peak District: England's first national park, created in 1951, in the southern Pennines, and nowhere near Scotland.
Places in Scotland.Windermere: England's largest natural lake, in the Lake District, and Beatrix Potter's neighborhood.
Places in Scotland.Brecon Beacons: A Welsh national park of high peaks and a dark sky reserve, also known as Bannau Brycheiniog.

Parts of the digestive system.Mouth: Digestion starts here: saliva contains amylase, an enzyme that begins breaking starch into sugar while you chew.
Parts of the digestive system.Esophagus: The esophagus is about 25 cm long and uses wave-like muscle squeezes, so you can swallow even upside down.
Parts of the digestive system.Stomach: Stomach acid has a pH around 1 to 2, strong enough to dissolve metal, and the lining renews every few days to protect itself.
Parts of the digestive system.Small intestine: The small intestine is about 6 meters long, and its folds give it a surface area often compared to a tennis court.
Parts of the digestive system.Large intestine: The large intestine is shorter but wider at about 1.5 meters. It mostly absorbs water and houses trillions of gut bacteria.
Parts of the digestive system.Liver: The liver makes bile for fat digestion and handles hundreds of other jobs. It is the only organ that can regrow substantially.
Parts of the digestive system.Pancreas: The pancreas makes enzymes to break down food and insulin to manage blood sugar, so it serves two systems at once.
Parts of the digestive system.Gallbladder: The gallbladder stores bile made by the liver and squirts it out when you eat fat. People can live without it.
Parts of the digestive system.Duodenum: The duodenum is the first stretch of the small intestine, only about 25 cm long, where bile and pancreatic juices join food.
Parts of the digestive system.Colon: The colon is the main part of the large intestine, where leftover waste loses its water and is formed into stool.
Parts of the digestive system.Salivary glands: You have three pairs of major salivary glands, and together they make about a liter of saliva every day.
Parts of the digestive system.Lungs: The lungs breathe, not digest. They are part of the respiratory system, though food that goes down the wrong way can reach them.
Parts of the digestive system.Heart: The heart pumps blood, so it is circulatory, not digestive. It beats about 100,000 times a day without a rest.
Parts of the digestive system.Kidneys: Kidneys filter blood and make urine, so they belong to the urinary system, not digestion.
Parts of the digestive system.Bladder: The bladder only stores urine. It holds about half a liter or more before you feel the urge.
Parts of the digestive system.Trachea: The trachea is the windpipe, for air. The epiglottis flaps shut over it when you swallow to keep food out.
Parts of the digestive system.Spleen: The spleen filters blood and stores immune cells. It sits near the stomach but is not part of digestion.
Parts of the digestive system.Thyroid: The thyroid, in the neck, sets metabolism through hormones, but it does not handle food directly.
Parts of the digestive system.Larynx: The larynx, or voice box, holds your vocal cords and sits in the airway, not in the digestive route.
Parts of the digestive system.Aorta: The aorta is the body's largest artery, and it carries blood away from the heart. It plays no part in digestion.
Parts of the digestive system.Diaphragm: The diaphragm is the muscle under the lungs that powers breathing. It's not part of the gut.
Parts of the digestive system.Brain: The brain does control hunger and swallowing, but it is part of the nervous system, not the digestive tract.
Parts of the digestive system.Tonsils: Tonsils sit at the back of the throat and help immunity. They are lymphatic tissue, not part of digestion.
Parts of the digestive system.Ureter: The ureter is a tube taking urine from kidney to bladder. It belongs to the urinary system.

Biodegradable materials.Banana peel: A peel can take a few weeks to months to break down, far longer in cold climates. Tossing it outdoors isn't harmless litter, especially on trails.
Biodegradable materials.Paper: Paper made from wood fibers breaks down in a few months, and it's one of the most recycled materials, reused around five to seven times.
Biodegradable materials.Cotton shirt: Cotton is plant cellulose, so soil microbes digest it in months. Buried cotton underwear is a real test farmers use to gauge soil health.
Biodegradable materials.Wool sock: Wool is made of keratin, the protein in hair and nails, and it decomposes in soil within a year or so, releasing nitrogen.
Biodegradable materials.Leaves: Fallen leaves feed fungi and bacteria that turn them into humus, which is how forests recycle their own nutrients every autumn.
Biodegradable materials.Wood: Fungi, termites and bacteria break wood down, but dry wood in a dry place can last for thousands of years, as Egyptian furniture shows.
Biodegradable materials.Apple core: An apple core rots in a few weeks, and apple seeds contain a little cyanide-releasing compound. Don't worry, you'd need many of them.
Biodegradable materials.Eggshell: Eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate and break down in soil over time. Gardeners crush them to add calcium for plants.
Biodegradable materials.Bread: Bread molds in days and fully decays quickly, but moldy slices outdoors can attract rats and pests, so compost it carefully.
Biodegradable materials.Cardboard: Cardboard is layered paper pulp and breaks down in a few months, which is why gardeners lay it down to smother weeds.
Biodegradable materials.Hemp rope: Hemp fiber was once used for ships' ropes and sails, and rots naturally when left damp. The word 'canvas' comes from cannabis.
Biodegradable materials.Plastic bag: A bag can persist for centuries in some environments, breaking into microplastics rather than truly decomposing.
Biodegradable materials.Styrofoam: Foam is polystyrene filled with about 95 percent air. It crumbles into pieces but doesn't truly biodegrade, lasting for centuries.
Biodegradable materials.Glass bottle: Glass is made mainly from sand and doesn't biodegrade, but it's endlessly recyclable without loss of quality.
Biodegradable materials.Aluminum can: Aluminum can take around 200 years to corrode away, but recycling one saves roughly 95 percent of the energy needed to make a new can.
Biodegradable materials.Nylon: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fiber, introduced in the 1930s. Its plastic makeup means microbes largely can't digest it.
Biodegradable materials.Polyester: Polyester is plastic made from petroleum, so it persists. Each wash can shed tiny microfibers into waterways.
Biodegradable materials.Car tire: Tires combine synthetic rubber, steel and chemicals, and they last for decades or longer. They're a major source of microplastics.
Biodegradable materials.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap began in 1957 as an attempt at textured wallpaper. It's polyethylene plastic, which won't biodegrade in any practical timeframe.
Biodegradable materials.Plastic straw: A plastic straw may take hundreds of years to break down, one reason many cities and restaurants have moved to paper alternatives.
Biodegradable materials.Light bulb: Glass, metal and other parts of bulbs don't biodegrade, and CFL bulbs contain mercury, so they need special disposal.
Biodegradable materials.Steel can: A steel can rusts in decades, and steel is the most recycled material in the world. Rusting is chemical, not biological, so it isn't biodegradation.
Biodegradable materials.Ceramic mug: Fired clay is practically permanent, which is why archaeologists dig up pottery shards thousands of years old.
Biodegradable materials.PVC pipe: PVC is tough plastic that resists rot, which makes it great for plumbing but terrible for biodegradation. It can persist for centuries.

Justice League members.Superman: Created in 1938 by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, he debuted in Action Comics #1 and launched the superhero genre.
Justice League members.Batman: He has no powers, only training and wealth; Bob Kane and Bill Finger created him in 1939.
Justice League members.Wonder Woman: Her creator, William Moulton Marston, also helped invent an early lie detector, which inspired her Lasso of Truth.
Justice League members.The Flash: Barry Allen's 1956 debut is often credited with starting the Silver Age of comics.
Justice League members.Aquaman: The 2018 film grossed over a billion dollars, but the character dates back to 1941.
Justice League members.Green Lantern: His power ring, in classic stories, could not affect anything yellow.
Justice League members.Cyborg: Victor Stone was created in 1980 for the New Teen Titans and joined the League as a founding member in the 2011 reboot.
Justice League members.Martian Manhunter: J'onn J'onzz is a Martian shapeshifter and founding member in the comics; fire is his great weakness.
Justice League members.Green Arrow: Oliver Queen is a billionaire archer with no powers, and his trick arrows make him a sort of Batman with a bow.
Justice League members.Hawkgirl: In the animated series, she is an alien police officer from Thanagar who wields a mace.
Justice League members.Black Canary: Dinah Lance's Canary Cry is a sonic scream, and she is also a martial artist; she debuted in 1947.
Justice League members.Iron Man: Tony Stark is Marvel, not DC; his 2008 film launched the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Justice League members.Captain America: Marvel's WWII supersoldier debuted in 1941 on a cover that shows him punching Hitler.
Justice League members.Thor: Thor is Marvel's Norse thunder god; only the worthy can lift his hammer Mjolnir.
Justice League members.Hulk: Marvel's green giant was inspired by Jekyll and Hyde and Frankenstein; in his first issue he was gray.
Justice League members.Black Widow: Natasha Romanoff is Marvel, not DC; she debuted in a 1964 Iron Man story as a Soviet villain.
Justice League members.Hawkeye: Marvel's archer, often compared to Green Arrow, but he's an Avenger, not a League member.
Justice League members.Spider-Man: Marvel's wall-crawler did meet Superman in a famous 1976 crossover comic, but he is not a League member.
Justice League members.Doctor Strange: Marvel's Sorcerer Supreme; DC's nearest equivalent is Doctor Fate.
Justice League members.Black Panther: T'Challa debuted in 1966 as Marvel's first Black superhero in mainstream comics, before the Black Panther Party was founded.
Justice League members.Vision: An android built by Ultron and an Avenger; he belongs to Marvel, not the Justice League.
Justice League members.Scarlet Witch: Wanda Maximoff debuted in 1964 as a villain in the X-Men; she's Marvel through and through.
Justice League members.Ant-Man: Hank Pym's shrinking hero was a founding Avenger in 1963, not a Justice League member.
Justice League members.Star-Lord: Peter Quill leads Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy; DC's own space hero is Green Lantern.

Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Po: The panda who dreams of being a kung fu hero; Jack Black voiced him in the 2008 hit. His ordinary dumpling-loving self is his secret strength.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Master Shifu: The red panda who trains the Furious Five. Dustin Hoffman voiced him, and he is not actually a panda, which is a running joke.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Tigress: The tiger who is the strongest of the Furious Five. Angelina Jolie voices her, and Tigress is the team's fierce, serious leader.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Monkey: Monkey is one of the Furious Five. Jackie Chan voiced him in the films, nodding to the real Monkey style of kung fu.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Mantis: The insect of the Furious Five. He fits the praying mantis style, which is based on a real Chinese martial art.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Viper: A snake with a flower on her head, Viper is the gentlest of the Furious Five. Lucy Liu voiced her.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Crane: Crane is the gentlest of the Five, a nervous flier who is Po's friend. David Cross voiced him, and the film borrows from the real Crane style.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Tai Lung: A snow leopard and Shifu's former student, who turned to evil. He escapes prison in the first film.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Oogway: A wise old tortoise who chose Po as Dragon Warrior. His name is Chinese for Turtle, with a nod to the old teachers of kung fu legend.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Mr. Ping: Po's adoptive father, a goose who runs a noodle shop. The joke is that a goose has raised a panda, which was the film's best running gag.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Lord Shen: A peacock and the villain of the second film, who invented a cannon to conquer China. Gary Oldman voiced him.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Kai: A yak spirit warrior who steals chi, the villain of the third film. J.K. Simmons voiced him.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.The Chameleon: A shape-shifting lizard who is the villain of the fourth film. Viola Davis voiced her.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Mushu: Mushu is a small dragon from Disney's Mulan, not Kung Fu Panda. Eddie Murphy voiced him, and he is a demoted family guardian.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Cri-Kee: The lucky cricket in Mulan, not Kung Fu Panda. He is a tiny insect sidekick, like Mantis but from a different film.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Shan Yu: Shan Yu is the Hun leader in Disney's Mulan, not a Kung Fu Panda villain. His pet falcon is a recognizable mark.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Li Shang: Captain Li Shang is Mulan's commander and love interest, not part of the Furious Five. He is from a different film.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Mulan: The heroine of Disney's Mulan, who disguises herself as a man. She fights, but not in the Valley of Peace.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Mr. Miyagi: Mr. Miyagi trains Daniel in The Karate Kid, a different series, though his wax on, wax off drills echo Shifu's ways.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Splinter: The rat master who trains the Ninja Turtles, a different martial arts series. Like Shifu, he is a small mentor.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Raya: The heroine of Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon, set in a fantasy Southeast Asia. A fighter but not in the Valley of Peace.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Sisu: The dragon in Raya and the Last Dragon, voiced by Awkwafina. A dragon, but from another film.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Yoda: Yoda is a small green Jedi master from Star Wars, a mentor in the same mold as Oogway, but from another galaxy. Frank Oz voices him.
Characters in Kung Fu Panda.Daniel LaRusso: The student in The Karate Kid who learns from Mr. Miyagi. He is not in Kung Fu Panda.

Woodwind instruments.Flute: A modern concert flute is almost always metal, yet it's a woodwind, because the sound is made by air alone and not by a reed.
Woodwind instruments.Clarinet: A single-reed instrument with a wide range, and Mozart wrote his final concerto for it in 1791, shortly before he died.
Woodwind instruments.Oboe: Its double reed produces a piercing tone, and the orchestra tunes to the oboe's A before a concert.
Woodwind instruments.Bassoon: A double-reed instrument with about 9 feet of folded tubing, and its voice is deep and reedy.
Woodwind instruments.Saxophone: Despite its brass body, it is a woodwind, because it uses a single reed. Adolphe Sax patented it in 1846.
Woodwind instruments.Piccolo: Half the size of a flute, it plays an octave higher, and can be heard above a full orchestra.
Woodwind instruments.Recorder: A staple of school music, the recorder was a serious instrument in Baroque Europe, and Bach and Handel wrote for it.
Woodwind instruments.English horn: It's neither English nor a horn: it is a larger relative of the oboe, with a pear-shaped bell, and has a hauntingly mellow voice.
Woodwind instruments.Contrabassoon: It plays an octave lower than a bassoon, with a tube of about 16 feet folded into itself, and is among the lowest instruments in the orchestra.
Woodwind instruments.Bass clarinet: A clarinet that plays an octave lower than the regular one and it has a curved metal neck and an upturned bell.
Woodwind instruments.Pan flute: Made from tubes of different lengths bound together, it's blown across the tops, and it's associated with the Greek god Pan, though it's much older.
Woodwind instruments.Trumpet: A brass instrument in which the player's lips buzz into a cup mouthpiece, which sets it apart from a woodwind's reed or air stream.
Woodwind instruments.Trombone: A brass instrument with a slide, and its sound comes from buzzing lips, not from a reed.
Woodwind instruments.Tuba: The orchestra's lowest brass instrument, which is not a woodwind. It's made of about 18 feet of coiled brass tubing.
Woodwind instruments.French horn: A coiled brass instrument played with buzzing lips, and its hand-in-the-bell technique makes it unique, but not a woodwind.
Woodwind instruments.Cornet: A short, compact brass instrument that is a close cousin of the trumpet, with a mellow tone.
Woodwind instruments.Bugle: A valveless brass instrument associated with military calls such as Taps, with no reed and no woodwind connection.
Woodwind instruments.Euphonium: A tenor-voiced brass instrument often in military bands, whose sound comes from buzzing lips and not a reed.
Woodwind instruments.Violin: A bowed string instrument, so its sound comes from vibrating strings and not from a reed or air column.
Woodwind instruments.Harp: A plucked string instrument, so it sits with strings, not woodwinds, because no reed or blown air is involved.
Woodwind instruments.Xylophone: A percussion instrument with wooden bars struck by mallets, so nothing is blown through it.
Woodwind instruments.Snare drum: A percussion instrument whose wires, the snares, are stretched on the bottom head for a crisp rattle.
Woodwind instruments.Glockenspiel: A percussion instrument with metal bars, whose name is German for 'bell play', and not blown at all.
Woodwind instruments.Sousaphone: A marching tuba named for John Philip Sousa, wrapped around the player's body, and brass because lips buzz in a cup.

Motor races.Daytona 500: NASCAR's season opener at Daytona International Speedway in Florida, where cars run in packs at close to 200 mph on high banks.
Motor races.Indy 500: A race of 200 laps around the Indianapolis oval, where winners drink milk, a tradition begun in 1936.
Motor races.24 Hours of Le Mans: The endurance classic in France tests cars and drivers over a whole day and night, with the winner covering over 5,000 km.
Motor races.Monaco Grand Prix: A Formula 1 street race with the sport's slowest, tightest corners; it is part of motorsport's unofficial Triple Crown.
Motor races.Dakar Rally: Originally Paris-Dakar, it has been run in South America and Saudi Arabia since security worries cancelled the 2008 African edition.
Motor races.Isle of Man TT: Motorbikes race the 37-mile Mountain Course on closed public roads, with average speeds beyond 130 mph for the fastest laps.
Motor races.Bathurst 1000: Australia's great touring-car race runs 1,000 km up and down Mount Panorama, and its Conrod Straight is a famous test of top speed.
Motor races.Pikes Peak: A hill climb in Colorado, up a 12.4-mile road with about 150 corners, finishing at 14,000 feet where thin air saps engine power.
Motor races.Baja 1000: An off-road race in Mexico's Baja California peninsula, open to cars, trucks and bikes, and usually run as a point-to-point or loop across desert.
Motor races.Brickyard 400: A NASCAR race at Indianapolis Motor Speedway, nicknamed for the bricks that once paved the track, and a strip of them remains at the finish line.
Motor races.British Grand Prix: The world championship's host since 1950, held at Silverstone, a former wartime airfield.
Motor races.Sebring 12 Hours: A Florida endurance race held on a bumpy former airbase, famous for being rough on cars, with the 12 hours starting in the day.
Motor races.Kentucky Derby: A race for three-year-old horses, run at Churchill Downs, with winners draped in a blanket of roses.
Motor races.Grand National: A horse steeplechase over huge fences at Aintree, a sport where jockeys, not drivers, risk life and limb.
Motor races.Tour de France: A bike race rather than motor racing: riders cover about 3,500 km over three weeks, powered only by their legs.
Motor races.Iditarod: A dog-sled race across Alaska; its engines are huskies, not motors.
Motor races.Boston Marathon: A foot race run every April on Patriots' Day, and its field is made up of runners with qualifying times.
Motor races.Melbourne Cup: A horse race that halts Australia at 3 pm on the first Tuesday of November, for about three and a half minutes.
Motor races.The Boat Race: The Oxford and Cambridge rowing contest on the Thames, powered by eight oarsmen and a cox.
Motor races.America's Cup: Sailing's oldest international trophy, raced in cutting-edge boats that now fly above the water on foils, but with no engines.
Motor races.Giro d'Italia: One of cycling's three Grand Tours, run through Italy in May with riders wearing a pink jersey.
Motor races.Ironman: A triathlon: 3.8 km swim, 180 km cycle, then a marathon, and all of it done by the athlete's own power.
Motor races.Belmont Stakes: A horse race at Belmont Park, New York, run over a mile and a half, the longest of the Triple Crown races.
Motor races.Great North Run: A half marathon from Newcastle to South Shields, the biggest in the world, with tens of thousands of runners.

Nicknames of famous athletes.Air Jordan: Michael Jordan's nickname for his leaps led to Nike's shoe line, launched in 1985, which the NBA at first fined him for wearing.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Great One: Wayne Gretzky, whose 99 jersey is retired league-wide, and who famously said you miss 100 percent of the shots you don't take.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Bambino: Babe Ruth, an Italian nickname meaning baby, and a curse supposedly fell on Boston after he was sold to the Yankees in 1920.
Nicknames of famous athletes.King James: LeBron James, nicknamed since high school, who moved from Cleveland to Miami, back to Cleveland, and then to Los Angeles.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Golden Bear: Jack Nicklaus, who won a record 18 major golf championships, and whose blond hair and bulk inspired the name.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Iron Mike: Mike Tyson, the youngest heavyweight champion at 20, famous for a fearsome knockout power and a peekaboo defensive style.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Black Mamba: Kobe Bryant chose the name himself, after the deadly snake, and used it as an alter ego for fierce competition.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Refrigerator: William Perry, a huge Chicago Bears defensive tackle who also ran the ball in the 1986 Super Bowl, a play that thrilled fans.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Lightning Bolt: Usain Bolt, whose famous victory pose imitates the shape of a lightning strike, and his name suited the job.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Rocket: Used for several stars, including hockey's Maurice Richard, snooker's Ronnie O'Sullivan and Roger Clemens, all fast and explosive.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Sweetness: Walter Payton, the Bears running back, got it for his smooth grace on the field, despite his bruising running style.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Boss: Bruce Springsteen, a musician rather than an athlete, who got the name for collecting the band's pay on tour.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Ol' Blue Eyes: A nickname for Frank Sinatra, a singer, not an athlete, and not on a baseball card.
Nicknames of famous athletes.King of Pop: Michael Jackson, whose Thriller is one of the best-selling albums ever, and he's a singer, not a sportsman.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Queen of Soul: Aretha Franklin, the singer of Respect, a musician's title rather than a sports one.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Material Girl: Madonna, named after her 1984 hit, and she's a pop star, not an athlete.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Slowhand: Eric Clapton's nickname, a guitarist's title, and the joke was about a slow handclap from fans while he changed a string.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Satchmo: Louis Armstrong, the jazz trumpeter, short for satchel mouth, and not a sports nickname.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Duke: Used for John Wayne, an actor, and Duke Ellington, a jazz composer, not a sports figure.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Fonz: Henry Winkler's character on Happy Days, a fictional biker, and not an athlete.
Nicknames of famous athletes.The Bard: William Shakespeare's nickname, and the poet is the Bard of Avon, and no athlete is called that.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Rocket Man: Elton John's song title from 1972, used as his nickname, but not a sports star's name.
Nicknames of famous athletes.Godfather of Soul: James Brown, a singer famous for funk and hard-working dance moves, and not an athlete.

Legendary places never proven real.Atlantis: Plato described this island in two dialogues around 360 BC, and it sank in a day and night; he may have invented it as a moral tale.
Legendary places never proven real.El Dorado: It began as a gilded king who covered himself in gold dust in a Colombian lake ritual, then became a lost city that drew expeditions for centuries.
Legendary places never proven real.Shangri-La: James Hilton invented this hidden Himalayan paradise in his 1933 novel 'Lost Horizon'; several places now claim the name.
Legendary places never proven real.Avalon: The island where Arthur was taken to heal; medieval monks at Glastonbury claimed in 1191 to have found his grave.
Legendary places never proven real.Camelot: Arthur's court has no proven historic site, though Cadbury Castle in Somerset and others are suggested.
Legendary places never proven real.Lemuria: A lost continent proposed in the 1860s to explain lemur fossils across the Indian Ocean; plate tectonics made it obsolete.
Legendary places never proven real.Hyperborea: The Greeks imagined a sunny land beyond the north wind, where people lived a thousand years, and Apollo spent winters there.
Legendary places never proven real.Lyonesse: A Cornish legend of a land between Land's End and the Scilly Isles, now said to be under the sea; its church bells are said to still ring.
Legendary places never proven real.Agartha: A hollow-earth realm in 19th-century occult writing, claimed to be under Asia, with advanced beings.
Legendary places never proven real.Cibola: The Seven Cities of Gold that drew Coronado north in 1540; he found only Zuni pueblos.
Legendary places never proven real.Troy: A trap: it was real; Heinrich Schliemann dug at Hisarlik, Turkey, in the 1870s and found its ruins.
Legendary places never proven real.Pompeii: A trap: it's real, buried by Vesuvius's eruption in AD 79, and still being excavated.
Legendary places never proven real.Machu Picchu: A trap: it's real, an Inca estate built about 1450 and made known to the world by Hiram Bingham in 1911.
Legendary places never proven real.Petra: A trap: it's real, a Nabataean city carved into rose-red rock in Jordan.
Legendary places never proven real.Angkor: A trap: real, the Khmer capital in Cambodia with Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world.
Legendary places never proven real.Babylon: A trap: it's real, with ruins in Iraq, though the Hanging Gardens remain unproven.
Legendary places never proven real.Knossos: A trap: the real Minoan palace on Crete, excavated by Arthur Evans from 1900, tied to the Minotaur's labyrinth legend.
Legendary places never proven real.Mohenjo-daro: A trap: it's real, a city of the Indus Valley civilization in Pakistan, built around 2500 BC.
Legendary places never proven real.Ur: A trap: a real Sumerian city in Iraq, thought to be Abraham's birthplace.
Legendary places never proven real.Carthage: A trap: real, the Phoenician city in Tunisia that Rome destroyed in 146 BC.
Legendary places never proven real.Tikal: A trap: a real Maya city, whose temples rise above Guatemala's rainforest.
Legendary places never proven real.Nineveh: A trap: the real Assyrian capital near Mosul, with Ashurbanipal's library of clay tablets.
Legendary places never proven real.Great Zimbabwe: A trap: real, a stone city in Zimbabwe built by Shona ancestors, with walls standing about 11 metres high.
Legendary places never proven real.Jericho: A trap: real, and among the oldest continuously inhabited cities, for over 10,000 years.

Offices of ancient Rome.Consul: The chief annual magistrates, elected two at a time to share power and check one another. 'Consul' even gave its name to a year: dates were set by who held it.
Offices of ancient Rome.Senator: A member of the ruling advisory body, originally 'old men'. Senators had to own much land and could not hold trade jobs.
Offices of ancient Rome.Tribune: An official protecting ordinary citizens (plebeians), with the power of veto. Their person was sacred, and harming one was a serious crime.
Offices of ancient Rome.Praetor: A magistrate ranking just below the consuls, who led armies and ran the law courts. The number of praetors grew as Rome's empire did.
Offices of ancient Rome.Censor: An official who counted citizens and judged their morals, and could expel senators for misconduct. His term was 18 months.
Offices of ancient Rome.Quaestor: An entry-level financial magistrate looking after the treasury, and the first rung on the career ladder.
Offices of ancient Rome.Aedile: The magistrate who managed public games, markets and buildings. Many future politicians won votes by funding lavish shows.
Offices of ancient Rome.Dictator: A one-person ruler appointed in emergencies, for six months at most. Julius Caesar later made himself dictator for life, and was soon killed.
Offices of ancient Rome.Emperor: Augustus created the role in 27 BC while pretending to preserve the Republic. He called himself 'princeps', first citizen.
Offices of ancient Rome.Proconsul: A governor who held power after his year as consul, ruling a province or leading an army. Roman provinces were often run this way.
Offices of ancient Rome.Pharaoh: Trap: Egypt's ruler and a legitimate African title, but not a Roman office. Rome conquered Egypt in 30 BC.
Offices of ancient Rome.Shogun: Trap: Japan's hereditary military ruler of the 1100s to 1800s. A medieval Japanese office, with no Roman connection at all.
Offices of ancient Rome.Tsar: Trap: a Russian ruler's title, derived from Caesar, but used in Russia, not Rome itself.
Offices of ancient Rome.Caliph: Trap: the title of Muslim leaders succeeding Muhammad, from the 600s AD, centuries after Rome's republic.
Offices of ancient Rome.Daimyo: Trap: a Japanese feudal lord who served the shogun and commanded samurai. It's medieval Japan, a world away from Rome.
Offices of ancient Rome.Jarl: Trap: a Norse noble rank from the Viking Age, centuries after the fall of the Roman Republic. English 'earl' comes from it.
Offices of ancient Rome.Archon: Trap: a high magistrate in ancient Athens, where nine archons served each year. Greek, not Roman.
Offices of ancient Rome.Ephor: Trap: one of five elected officials in Sparta who checked the power of its two kings. Greek, not Roman.
Offices of ancient Rome.Doge: Trap: the elected leader of Venice for a thousand years until Napoleon ended it in 1797.
Offices of ancient Rome.Khan: Trap: a Mongol and Turkic ruler's title, which came into use long after Rome's Republic.
Offices of ancient Rome.Vizier: Trap: a senior minister in Islamic courts who ran the government for the caliph or sultan, not a Roman post.
Offices of ancient Rome.Mandarin: Trap: an imperial Chinese official, selected by exams. It was only later used in English for 'bureaucrat'.
Offices of ancient Rome.Satrap: Trap: a provincial governor in the Persian Empire, collecting taxes for the king. Rome had proconsuls, a different office.
Offices of ancient Rome.Sultan: Trap: an Islamic ruler's title, as for Ottoman sultans, which only arose in medieval times.

Eras of human history (not geological).Stone Age: The longest era, lasting millions of years, from the first stone tools to the arrival of metal. Humans spent most of their story in it.
Eras of human history (not geological).Bronze Age: Smiths mixed copper with tin to make a harder metal, and trade routes for tin became vital. It began around 3300 BC in places.
Eras of human history (not geological).Iron Age: Iron was harder to work than bronze but its ore is common, so tools and weapons became cheap. Dates vary widely by region.
Eras of human history (not geological).Middle Ages: The name was coined by later scholars who saw it as a gap between the classical world and their own time. It runs roughly from AD 500 to 1500.
Eras of human history (not geological).Renaissance: The word means 'rebirth', for the revival of classical learning that began in Italy in the 1300s and flowered in the 1400s and 1500s.
Eras of human history (not geological).Enlightenment: Also called the Age of Reason, this 1700s movement pressed reason and science against tradition and shaped modern ideas of rights.
Eras of human history (not geological).Victorian era: It is named for Queen Victoria, who reigned for 63 years, and marks industrial Britain, empire and huge social change.
Eras of human history (not geological).Jazz Age: Writer F. Scott Fitzgerald is credited with naming the 1920s, a decade of new music, new freedoms and big spending.
Eras of human history (not geological).Belle Epoque: French for 'beautiful era', the late 1800s to 1914 in Europe was a time of optimism, art nouveau and the Eiffel Tower.
Eras of human history (not geological).Viking Age: From about 793 to 1066, Norse seafarers raided, traded and settled across Europe, and even reached North America.
Eras of human history (not geological).Edo period: From 1603 to 1868, Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns from Edo, now Tokyo, and mostly closed to outsiders.
Eras of human history (not geological).Jurassic: Trap: it is a geological period about 200 to 145 million years ago, when dinosaurs ruled. Humans came far later.
Eras of human history (not geological).Cretaceous: Trap: a geologic period that ended 66 million years ago with the dinosaur extinction. Its name comes from the Latin for chalk.
Eras of human history (not geological).Triassic: Trap: a geologic period starting about 252 million years ago after the worst mass extinction, when dinosaurs first appeared.
Eras of human history (not geological).Cambrian: Trap: a geologic period starting about 539 million years ago, famous for the sudden burst of animal diversity.
Eras of human history (not geological).Mesozoic: Trap: this geological era of the dinosaurs contains the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.
Eras of human history (not geological).Pleistocene: Trap: the geological epoch of the ice ages, up to about 11,700 years ago. Humans exist in it, but it is a geological time unit.
Eras of human history (not geological).Holocene: Trap: the geological epoch we live in, starting about 11,700 years ago. Human history happens within it, but it's a geologic term.
Eras of human history (not geological).Permian: Trap: a geologic period ending about 252 million years ago in the biggest mass extinction ever.
Eras of human history (not geological).Devonian: Trap: the geologic 'Age of Fishes', about 419 to 359 million years ago, named for Devon in England.
Eras of human history (not geological).Paleozoic: Trap: a geological era of 'old life' running from about 539 to 252 million years ago.
Eras of human history (not geological).Cenozoic: Trap: the geological era of mammals, which began 66 million years ago and is still going.
Eras of human history (not geological).Silurian: Trap: a geological period about 444 to 419 million years ago, named for an ancient Welsh tribe, the Silures.
Eras of human history (not geological).Ordovician: Trap: a geological period around 485 to 444 million years ago, also named for a Welsh tribe, the Ordovices.

Household chores.Vacuuming: The first powered vacuum cleaner was built in 1901 by Hubert Cecil Booth in London and was so big it was drawn by horses.
Household chores.Dusting: Much household dust is actually shed human skin and fibers, along with outdoor pollen and soil.
Household chores.Mopping: Mopping has been around for centuries, and the first squeeze mop with a bucket arrived in the late 1800s.
Household chores.Ironing: Before electricity, irons were solid chunks of metal heated on the stove, which is why they were called sad irons.
Household chores.Doing laundry: Laundry once meant beating clothes on rocks, and the electric washing machine only became common in the 1900s.
Household chores.Washing dishes: Washing by hand can use more water than a modern dishwasher, which uses a few gallons of water for a full load.
Household chores.Making the bed: A study found that people who make the bed often feel more productive, though dust mites like damp, unmade sheets.
Household chores.Taking out the trash: The average American produces about four and a half pounds of trash per day, so the bin fills quickly.
Household chores.Mowing the lawn: The lawn mower was invented in 1830 by Edwin Budding, an English engineer who got the idea from a cloth-trimming machine.
Household chores.Sweeping: Brooms were once made from twigs, and the flat broom of the Shakers appeared in the early 1800s.
Household chores.Folding clothes: Marie Kondo popularized folding clothes into small upright rectangles so they can be seen at a glance in a drawer.
Household chores.Cleaning windows: The squeegee was invented in 1936 by Ettore Steccone, who was a window cleaner, and it is still the pro's tool.
Household chores.Watching TV: TV is leisure, and the average American watches roughly three hours a day, which is far more than they spend cleaning.
Household chores.Napping: A short nap of 10 to 20 minutes can boost alertness, but is a rest, not a chore.
Household chores.Jogging: Jogging is exercise, not a chore, and the word became popular in the 1960s after Bill Bowerman's book Jogging brought it to Americans.
Household chores.Reading a novel: Reading is a pastime and the novel is a form that took off in the 1700s with writers like Daniel Defoe.
Household chores.Knitting: Knitting is a hobby, and the oldest known knitted items, socks, were found in Egypt from around the 11th century.
Household chores.Playing chess: Chess is a game, and it is likely over 1,500 years old, from a game called chaturanga in India.
Household chores.Sunbathing: Sunbathing is leisure, and a short time in sun makes vitamin D, though too much risks skin damage.
Household chores.Video gaming: Gaming is play, and the 1972 game Pong helped start a multibillion dollar industry.
Household chores.Bowling: Bowling is a sport; the earliest evidence of it comes from ancient Egypt, with a game found in a child's tomb.
Household chores.Texting: The first text message was sent in December 1992 and read Merry Christmas.
Household chores.Daydreaming: Daydreaming is not a chore, and the brain is surprisingly active, using what scientists call the default mode network.
Household chores.Doing yoga: Yoga is exercise, and its practice goes back over 2,000 years in India, long before today's studios.

Eye conditions.Cataract: A cloudy lens, and cataract removal with an artificial lens implant is among the safest surgeries done.
Eye conditions.Glaucoma: Pressure damages the optic nerve, often with no symptoms early, so regular eye exams catch it.
Eye conditions.Astigmatism: An unevenly curved cornea or lens blurs vision, and the name comes from Greek for 'without a point'.
Eye conditions.Myopia: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is increasing worldwide, and time outdoors seems to protect children's eyes.
Eye conditions.Pink eye: Pink eye is inflammation of the eye's clear covering, and viral forms spread easily among kids.
Eye conditions.Stye: A stye is a painful bump on the eyelid from an infected oil gland, and warm compresses help.
Eye conditions.Color blindness: Roughly 1 in 12 men have some form of color vision deficiency, compared to about 1 in 200 women.
Eye conditions.Lazy eye: Amblyopia means the brain favors one eye, and treating it in childhood works much better than later.
Eye conditions.Nearsightedness: Nearsighted people see close things clearly and far things blurry, because the eyeball is slightly too long.
Eye conditions.Farsightedness: Farsightedness makes close objects blurry, and many young people compensate by focusing harder, which causes headaches.
Eye conditions.Dry eye: Staring at screens reduces blinking, one big reason dry eye is so common now.
Eye conditions.Tinnitus: A trap: tinnitus is a ringing in the ears, so it belongs with hearing, not sight.
Eye conditions.Vertigo: Vertigo is a spinning sensation usually from the inner ear, and Hitchcock's film made the word famous.
Eye conditions.Gingivitis: Gingivitis inflames gums, so it is a dental issue rather than an eye one.
Eye conditions.Tonsillitis: Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils in the throat, not the eye.
Eye conditions.Eczema: Eczema is an itchy skin condition, though eyelid skin can be affected.
Eye conditions.Asthma: Asthma is a lung condition that narrows the airways.
Eye conditions.Bunion: A bunion is a bony bump at the base of the big toe, nowhere near the eyes.
Eye conditions.Earache: An earache is an ear problem, often from infection, especially common in small children.
Eye conditions.Laryngitis: Laryngitis is inflamed vocal cords, which leaves you hoarse or voiceless.
Eye conditions.Sinusitis: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, the air pockets in the skull around the nose.
Eye conditions.Scoliosis: Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine, commonly spotted in adolescents.
Eye conditions.Psoriasis: Psoriasis is an autoimmune skin disease that speeds up skin cell turnover, producing scaly patches.
Eye conditions.Cavity: A cavity is tooth decay, so it's a mouth matter instead of an eye one.

Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Breeze: A breeze can be a Beaufort force 2 to 3 wind, light enough to feel on your face and move leaves.
Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Freeze: Water is unusual because it expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats and pipes can burst in winter.
Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Knees: A knee is the largest joint in the body, and the kneecap acts as a pulley for the thigh muscles.
Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Please: Please comes from Latin placere, to be pleasing, and in French s'il vous plait literally means if it pleases you.

Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Keys: The modern pin-tumbler lock design was patented by Linus Yale Jr. in the 1860s and is still the basis for most keys.
Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Trees: Trees can communicate and share nutrients with others through fungal networks in the soil, nicknamed the wood wide web.
Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Fleas: A flea can jump over 100 times its own body length, making it one of the best jumpers for its size.
Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Squeeze: Squeeze comes from the Old English cwysan, meaning to crush, and its qu spelling later settled into squ.

Words that rhyme with 'sneeze'.Sense: Sense has similar letters at the start but ends in ens, so it is not a rhyme for sneeze.
