Baby milestones.Crawling: Crawling is not universal: some babies skip it entirely and go straight to scooting or walking, and that is fine.
Baby milestones.First steps: Most babies take their first steps between 9 and 15 months, and walking at 18 months is still normal.
Baby milestones.Teething: Babies are born with all of their baby teeth already formed inside the gums, and the first usually emerges around six months.
Baby milestones.Babbling: Babies start babbling around six months, and deaf babies exposed to sign language babble with their hands.
Baby milestones.Rolling over: Rolling over usually arrives by around four to six months, and it is the first big step in independent movement.
Baby milestones.First smile: A real social smile in response to a face typically appears around six to eight weeks, and sleepy smiles before that are reflexes.
Baby milestones.First word: First words typically appear around the first birthday, and they are often mama, dada, or a familiar sound like ba.
Baby milestones.Sitting up: Most babies sit without support by about six months, and the strength comes from tummy time and back muscles.
Baby milestones.Waving bye-bye: Waving goodbye is a social milestone around nine to twelve months, and it shows a baby understands gestures.
Baby milestones.Learning to drive: Learning to drive is a teenage milestone, not a baby one, and in many places begins at sixteen.
Baby milestones.Voting: Voting is a rite of adulthood, and in most democracies you must be 18, though a few countries allow 16.
Baby milestones.Graduating: Graduating is a late milestone and the word comes from Latin gradus, meaning step.
Baby milestones.Puberty: Puberty typically begins between ages 8 and 14, so it is a child-to-teen milestone, not a baby one.
Baby milestones.Retiring: Retiring is a milestone for the old, and the first national pension was set up in Germany in the 1880s.
Baby milestones.First shave: A first shave is for adolescents, and in some cultures it is a meaningful coming-of-age ritual.
Baby milestones.Getting married: Getting married is an adult milestone, and the average age varies widely, from late teens to over 30 around the world.
Baby milestones.First job: A first job is a teenager's milestone, and many people start with paper routes or summer work.
Baby milestones.Losing baby teeth: Losing baby teeth begins around age six, which is a child's milestone, not an infant's, and the first to go are usually the front ones.
Baby milestones.Learning to read: Learning to read usually comes at about age five to seven, so it is a childhood milestone rather than a baby one.
Baby milestones.Riding a bike: Riding a bike is often learned at five or six, which makes it a childhood milestone, not a baby milestone.
Baby milestones.Gray hair: Gray hair appears in adults when the cells that make pigment slow down, usually in the thirties onward.
Baby milestones.Tying shoelaces: Tying shoelaces is a childhood skill that commonly arrives at five or six years, long after babyhood.
Baby milestones.Getting braces: Braces are usually for kids and teens, around 10 to 14, once most adult teeth have come in.
Baby milestones.Voice cracking: A voice cracking is a puberty sign, as the larynx grows and the vocal cords thicken, and so isn't a baby milestone.

Things that have scales.Fish: Fish scales grow in layers like tree rings, and biologists can read them to estimate a fish's age.
Things that have scales.Snake: A snake's scales are made of keratin, the same material as your fingernails, and the skin is shed whole in one piece.
Things that have scales.Lizard: Lizard scales grow in overlapping layers and some species, like geckos, can drop their tails and regrow them.
Things that have scales.Crocodile: A crocodile's scaly skin has pressure-sensitive spots that can detect tiny ripples in the water, helping it find prey in darkness.
Things that have scales.Dragon: Dragons are mythical creatures, but real ones exist: the Komodo dragon is the largest lizard, up to about 3 meters long.
Things that have scales.Pangolin: The pangolin is the only mammal covered in scales, which are made of keratin, and it curls into a ball when threatened.
Things that have scales.Butterfly: A butterfly's wings are covered in thousands of tiny scales that make their colors, and the group name, Lepidoptera, means scaly wings.
Things that have scales.Map: A map has a scale, a key that tells how distances on paper relate to the real ground, so the word is a sense of scales.
Things that have scales.Moth: Moth wings are dusty because of the tiny scales, and those scales rub off easily on your fingers.
Things that have scales.Iguana: Iguanas have scaly skin and a spiny crest, and green iguanas in Florida sometimes fall from trees when cold snaps stun them.
Things that have scales.Gecko: Geckos have scales on their body and sticky toe pads with microscopic hairs that grip using weak molecular forces.
Things that have scales.Python: Pythons don't bite their prey to death; they squeeze it, and their scales help them grip as they climb and move.
Things that have scales.Frog: Frogs have smooth, moist skin that they partly breathe through, and it is why they must stay near water; there are no scales at all.
Things that have scales.Whale: Whales are mammals with smooth skin over thick blubber, and the blue whale is the largest animal ever, with no scales anywhere.
Things that have scales.Dolphin: Dolphins are smooth-skinned mammals, and their outer skin layer renews itself rapidly, replaced every few hours, helping them glide.
Things that have scales.Toad: Toads look scaly with bumpy, dry skin, but those bumps are glands, some of which ooze a bad-tasting toxin; they aren't scales.
Things that have scales.Octopus: An octopus is a boneless mollusk with soft skin and no scales, so it can squeeze through any gap larger than its hard beak.
Things that have scales.Salamander: Salamanders are amphibians with soft, moist skin and no scales, and some species can regrow lost limbs and even parts of the heart.
Things that have scales.Earthworm: Earthworms have soft, segmented bodies and breathe through their skin, which must stay damp, so there are no scales.
Things that have scales.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are about 95 percent water and have no bones, brain, or scales; some species have existed for hundreds of millions of years.
Things that have scales.Hippo: A hippo's thick skin has no scales; glands secrete a reddish oily fluid, nicknamed blood sweat, that works as sunscreen.
Things that have scales.Seal: Seals have fur or a sleek coat over a thick layer of blubber rather than scales, which keeps them warm in icy water.
Things that have scales.Squid: Squid have soft skin with color-changing cells and no scales, and a giant squid has the largest eyes of any animal, like dinner plates.
Things that have scales.Newt: A newt is an amphibian with smooth or slightly rough skin and no scales, and it can regrow limbs, eyes, and even parts of its heart.

Things with legs that can't walk.Table: A table has four legs, and the word 'tabletop' is more important, as tables go back to ancient Egypt.
Things with legs that can't walk.Chair: A chair has legs but can't walk, and chairs were once the privilege of high rank, hence the word 'chairman'.
Things with legs that can't walk.Stool: A stool is a seat with legs and no back, and three-legged stools stand steadily on uneven ground.
Things with legs that can't walk.Tripod: A tripod's three legs make it stable on uneven ground, since three points always define a flat plane.
Things with legs that can't walk.Pants: Pants have legs that hold feet but they can't walk, and we also call them trousers in British English.
Things with legs that can't walk.Easel: An easel's legs hold a canvas upright for painters, and the word comes from the Dutch word for donkey.
Things with legs that can't walk.Piano: A piano has three legs and a pedal lyre, and a grand piano's frame carries about 20 tons of string tension.
Things with legs that can't walk.Bed: A bed has legs to lift the mattress off the floor, and old four-poster beds also had tall posts.
Things with legs that can't walk.Desk: A desk has legs that hold up its writing surface, and the 'Resolute' desk in the Oval Office was made from a ship's timbers.
Things with legs that can't walk.Ironing board: An ironing board has folding legs, and the first adjustable one was patented in 1892 by Sarah Boone.
Things with legs that can't walk.Stepladder: A stepladder has two sets of legs, and its A-frame shape is what makes it freestanding.
Things with legs that can't walk.Rug: A rug has no legs, and the oldest known carpet, the Pazyryk, is about 2,500 years old.
Things with legs that can't walk.Pillow: A pillow has no legs and no spine, and its softness is why it fits in nearly every bed.
Things with legs that can't walk.Bowl: A bowl has no legs, and the earliest bowls were made from clay by hand thousands of years ago.
Things with legs that can't walk.Car: A car has wheels instead of legs, and 'horsepower' is a measure from when horses did the moving.
Things with legs that can't walk.Curtain: A curtain has no legs, and the word comes from the Latin for a court or enclosure.
Things with legs that can't walk.Book: A book has a spine, but not legs, and the longest spine reference is a novel's long story.
Things with legs that can't walk.Bucket: A bucket has a handle rather than legs, and it has been used since ancient times.
Things with legs that can't walk.Blanket: A blanket has no legs, and it's named after Thomas Blanket, a possible 14th-century weaver, though that's uncertain.
Things with legs that can't walk.Towel: A towel has no legs, and terry cloth made it more absorbent with its loops.
Things with legs that can't walk.Spoon: A spoon has a neck but no legs, and the oldest spoons were made from wood or shell.
Things with legs that can't walk.Vase: A vase has no legs, though some, like Greek amphorae, have two handles that look like ears.
Things with legs that can't walk.Umbrella: An umbrella has ribs, but it isn't standing on legs, and a stand holds it up.
Things with legs that can't walk.Hat: A hat has no legs, though the brim makes it look like it stands on a table.

Things an ant could carry.Bread crumb: A bread crumb weighs a few milligrams, and ants regularly haul pieces many times their own mass back to the nest.
Things an ant could carry.Sugar grain: A single sugar grain is a feast for an ant; ants can find sugar quickly, since they detect sweetness by smell.
Things an ant could carry.Grain of rice: A rice grain weighs roughly 20 milligrams, and a strong ant could manage that, since it can lift 10 to 50 times its weight.
Things an ant could carry.Sesame seed: A sesame seed weighs only a couple of milligrams, which makes it an easy haul for ants, which often carry them.
Things an ant could carry.Grain of sand: A grain of sand is a tiny speck of mostly quartz, light enough that even a single ant can drag it away easily.
Things an ant could carry.Poppy seed: A poppy seed is about a millimeter across, and it takes around a thousand to make a gram, so an ant can lift one.
Things an ant could carry.Cookie crumb: A cookie crumb is a common ant target, and the sugar and fat inside make it a rich load worth carrying home.
Things an ant could carry.Salt crystal: A salt crystal is a tiny cube of sodium chloride, and its perfect cube shape comes from the way the atoms stack.
Things an ant could carry.Tiny leaf bit: Leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaf many times their own size to farm fungus, which is what they actually eat.
Things an ant could carry.Dead gnat: A dead gnat is a lightweight meal, and ants are nature's cleanup crew, constantly hauling dead insects back to the nest.
Things an ant could carry.Watermelon: A watermelon is thousands of times heavier than an ant's strength, so even a swarm could not lift it.
Things an ant could carry.Brick: A brick weighs around two kilograms, which is millions of times more than a single ant could ever carry alone.
Things an ant could carry.Shoe: A shoe weighs far more than an ant can lift, though a whole colony could slowly drag a crumb of it.
Things an ant could carry.Apple: An apple weighs about 200 grams, which is far beyond what a single ant could lift, even with its great strength.
Things an ant could carry.Banana: A banana is far too heavy for a single ant, though a colony could eventually strip the sugar from a peel.
Things an ant could carry.Cat: A cat is millions of times heavier than an ant, and even a whole colony could not budge it.
Things an ant could carry.Phone: A phone weighs well over a hundred grams, far beyond the strength of any ant, even a champion lifter of leaves.
Things an ant could carry.Hammer: A hammer is heavy steel and wood, far too much for an ant, even though an ant can lift many times its own weight.
Things an ant could carry.Bicycle: A bicycle weighs about ten kilograms, and an ant carrying that would be like a person lifting a truck.
Things an ant could carry.Book: A book is far beyond an ant's strength, though ants will happily crawl along or live between its pages.
Things an ant could carry.Potato: A potato weighs well over a hundred grams, which is too much for an ant, though a colony will feast on a cut one.
Things an ant could carry.Football: A football weighs around 400 grams, millions of times more than an ant, so even a strong colony could not budge it.
Things an ant could carry.Pineapple: A pineapple weighs over a kilogram, far beyond what an ant can carry, though a colony may strip its sweet flesh.
Things an ant could carry.Laptop: A laptop weighs a couple of kilograms, way beyond an ant, even though ants scale up well for their size.

Things in a 1950s diner.Jukebox: The jukebox became a diner icon in the 1940s, when many ones played 78 rpm records.
Things in a 1950s diner.Milkshake: The milkshake started as an alcoholic drink in the 1880s, and the blended ice-cream version came in the 1920s.
Things in a 1950s diner.Neon sign: Neon signs were first displayed in Paris in 1910, and then spread into American diners.
Things in a 1950s diner.Booth: Booths, with their vinyl seats, were in diners from the start, many inspired by railway dining cars.
Things in a 1950s diner.Checkered floor: Black and white checkerboard floors are a diner trademark, and they hide dirt and look great.
Things in a 1950s diner.Burger: The hamburger name comes from Hamburg, Germany, but the sandwich took off in the US.
Things in a 1950s diner.French fries: French fries are likely Belgian in origin, and American soldiers in WWI called them French because of the local language.
Things in a 1950s diner.Soda fountain: Soda fountains were at first sold in pharmacies, where soda water was thought to be healthy.
Things in a 1950s diner.Counter stools: Counter stools let diners eat quickly and chat with the cook, and they often swivel.
Things in a 1950s diner.Apple pie: Apple pie as an American symbol came by the 1900s, though the dish was brought from Europe.
Things in a 1950s diner.Malted milk: Malted milk powder was invented in the 1870s by William Horlick, and malts are a diner favorite.
Things in a 1950s diner.Smartphone: Smartphones came in the 2000s, long after the 1950s, and the jukebox was the entertainment then.
Things in a 1950s diner.Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi was invented in the 1990s, so the 1950s diner had no wireless anything.
Things in a 1950s diner.Avocado toast: Avocado toast is a 2010s trend, and in the 1950s most Americans hadn't tried an avocado.
Things in a 1950s diner.Bubble tea: Bubble tea began in Taiwan in the 1980s, so a 1950s diner wouldn't have had any.
Things in a 1950s diner.Kombucha: Kombucha is an old fermented drink, but it only became trendy in the US in the 2000s.
Things in a 1950s diner.Touchscreen: Touchscreens arrived in the 1960s and spread in the 2000s, long after the diner's golden age.
Things in a 1950s diner.QR code menu: QR codes came in 1994 in Japan, from a car-parts company, so no diner menu had one in the 1950s.
Things in a 1950s diner.Smart TV: Smart TVs came in the 2010s, and 1950s diners had no TV at all, at least not usually.
Things in a 1950s diner.Self checkout: Self-checkout was introduced in the 1980s and spread in the 2000s, and the 1950s had a cashier.
Things in a 1950s diner.Oat milk latte: Oat milk lattes are a 2010s trend, as oat milk was developed in Sweden in the 1990s.
Things in a 1950s diner.Poke bowl: Poke bowls spread from Hawaii to the mainland US in the 2010s, and were not in 1950s diners.
Things in a 1950s diner.Laptop: Laptops came in the 1980s, and the first portable ones weighed a lot.
Things in a 1950s diner.Selfie stick: Selfie sticks were invented in the 1980s and exploded in the 2010s.

Things in a fire station.Fire engine: It carries hoses, ladders and a water pump. Many modern ones also carry medical gear, since most calls are medical.
Things in a fire station.Fire pole: Firefighters slide down it to reach trucks fast from upper floors. Many modern stations have dropped them for safety.
Things in a fire station.Fire hose: Big hoses move hundreds of gallons per minute. Their heavy canvas has been replaced mostly by tough synthetic fabrics.
Things in a fire station.Helmets: Traditional fire helmets have long rear brims that shed water. A leather design called the 'New Yorker' dates to the 1800s.
Things in a fire station.Axes: Used to chop through doors and roofs. The pick-head axe is one of a firefighter's most classic tools.
Things in a fire station.Turnout gear: The protective coat and trousers. It's named for how firefighters 'turned out' quickly to alarms.
Things in a fire station.Ladders: Fire ladders reach tall buildings. Aerial ladders on some trucks extend about 100 feet.
Things in a fire station.Siren: Warns traffic to clear the way. In Greek myth, Sirens lured sailors with song, giving the device its name.
Things in a fire station.Air tanks: Provide breathable air in smoke. A typical tank lasts roughly 30 minutes, depending on how hard the wearer works.
Things in a fire station.Bunk beds: Crews sleep at the station on 24-hour shifts, so bunks are standard, often with alarms to wake them.
Things in a fire station.Jail cell: Belongs in a police station or prison. A fire station doesn't hold prisoners.
Things in a fire station.Courtroom: Where judges hear cases. It's at a courthouse.
Things in a fire station.Mail sorter: Found at post offices. It's not part of a fire station.
Things in a fire station.Library books: Libraries hold books for loan. A fire station might have manuals, but not shelves of them.
Things in a fire station.Altar: Found in churches and temples. Not in firehouses.
Things in a fire station.Cash register: A shop item to ring up sales. Fire stations don't sell anything.
Things in a fire station.Operating table: For surgery, in hospitals. A fire station has no surgeons.
Things in a fire station.Blackboard: A school staple. Firefighters train, but the station seldom has chalk-based classrooms.
Things in a fire station.Church pews: Seating for congregations. Not at fire stations.
Things in a fire station.Runway: Where aircraft take off. An airport has fire stations, but the strip isn't in one.
Things in a fire station.Slot machine: Casino game. Fire stations don't host gambling.
Things in a fire station.Roulette wheel: A casino staple. It's not firehouse equipment.
Things in a fire station.Dentist's drill: Used in dental clinics. A fire station doesn't have one.
Things in a fire station.Bowling lane: Found in bowling alleys. Not in fire stations.

Arthurian legend characters.King Arthur: King Arthur first appears as a full-fledged king in Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century History of the Kings of Britain.
Arthurian legend characters.Merlin: Merlin, the wizard, was largely invented by Geoffrey of Monmouth, who adapted him from a Welsh prophet.
Arthurian legend characters.Lancelot: Lancelot is the knight who was added to the legend in the 12th century by Chrétien de Troyes, and who loves Guinevere.
Arthurian legend characters.Guinevere: Guinevere is Arthur's queen, whose love for Lancelot, in many tellings, brings down Camelot.
Arthurian legend characters.Gawain: Gawain, Arthur's nephew, is the knight who faces the Green Knight's beheading challenge.
Arthurian legend characters.Galahad: Galahad, Lancelot's pure son, is the knight in many versions who finally achieves the Holy Grail.
Arthurian legend characters.Percival: Percival is a knight of the Grail quest, who in early tellings fails to ask the crucial question.
Arthurian legend characters.Mordred: Mordred is Arthur's treacherous nephew or son who seizes the crown and mortally wounds him at Camlann.
Arthurian legend characters.Morgan le Fay: Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister, an enchantress who both helps and plots against him.
Arthurian legend characters.Lady of the Lake: The Lady of the Lake is the water spirit who, in some versions, gives Arthur Excalibur.
Arthurian legend characters.Tristan: Tristan is the knight who loves Isolde, in a romance that Wagner turned into a famous opera.
Arthurian legend characters.Isolde: Isolde is the Irish princess who falls for Tristan after they drink a love potion by mistake.
Arthurian legend characters.Bedivere: Bedivere is the knight who is told to throw Excalibur into the lake after Arthur's last battle.
Arthurian legend characters.Uther Pendragon: Uther Pendragon is Arthur's father, who with Merlin's magic disguises himself as Gorlois to be with Igraine.
Arthurian legend characters.Robin Hood: Robin Hood is an English outlaw from a separate legend, based in Sherwood Forest rather than Camelot.
Arthurian legend characters.Maid Marian: Maid Marian is Robin Hood's love, and she is not found in the earliest ballads.
Arthurian legend characters.Friar Tuck: Friar Tuck is the portly, fighting friar in Robin Hood's band, not part of the Round Table.
Arthurian legend characters.Little John: Little John is Robin Hood's giant lieutenant, ironically named, and a Sherwood outlaw.
Arthurian legend characters.Beowulf: Beowulf is an Old English poem's hero, a Geat who fights monsters, not Arthurian at all.
Arthurian legend characters.Siegfried: Siegfried is the dragon-slaying hero of the Nibelungenlied, a Germanic legend, not Arthurian.
Arthurian legend characters.Roland: Roland is Charlemagne's paladin, who dies at Roncesvalles in the Song of Roland, a French epic.
Arthurian legend characters.El Cid: El Cid was a real 11th-century Spanish knight, Rodrigo Díaz, who became the hero of an epic.
Arthurian legend characters.William Tell: William Tell is a Swiss crossbowman who shot an apple from his son's head, not an Arthurian figure.
Arthurian legend characters.Ivanhoe: Ivanhoe is the hero of Walter Scott's 1819 novel set in medieval England, with Robin Hood in a cameo.

Things that are spherical.Basketball: James Naismith invented the game in 1891 with a peach basket, and the early balls were soccer balls.
Things that are spherical.Marble: Glass marbles have been mass-produced since the 1890s, and the largest, the shooter, is also called a 'taw'.
Things that are spherical.Globe: The oldest surviving terrestrial globe, the Erdapfel, was made in Nuremberg in 1492, before Columbus's voyage mattered.
Things that are spherical.Pea: Peas are among the oldest cultivated crops, and a perfect sphere makes them easy to roll but also to spill.
Things that are spherical.Soap bubble: A bubble's surface tension pulls it into a sphere, because a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume.
Things that are spherical.Pearl: A pearl forms around an irritant inside an oyster, and natural ones that are round enough are rare.
Things that are spherical.Gumball: Gumball machines began in 1888 in New York, when Thomas Adams Gum put Tutti-Frutti balls in vending machines on train platforms.
Things that are spherical.Snowball: A snowball packs best near 0 degrees Celsius, when a thin film of water on the snow lets the flakes bond.
Things that are spherical.Disco ball: A mirror ball is covered in hundreds of small mirrors, and the first were used in dance halls in the 1920s.
Things that are spherical.Bowling ball: Standard ten-pin balls weigh up to 16 pounds, and many are made from reactive resin that grips the lane's oil.
Things that are spherical.Golf ball: The 300 to 500 dimples on a golf ball cut drag and let it fly roughly twice as far as a smooth one.
Things that are spherical.Ping-pong ball: The 40-millimeter table tennis ball is made of plastic since 2014, and was once made from celluloid.
Things that are spherical.Crystal ball: Fortune-tellers have gazed into these for centuries, and ones made of quartz are a staple of the fortune-teller's trade.
Things that are spherical.American football: It is a prolate spheroid, not a sphere, and the shape is partly a left over from rugby, which makes spirals possible.
Things that are spherical.Rugby ball: Rugby balls are oval because the first balls were made from pig's bladders, which are oval, inflated by hand.
Things that are spherical.Egg: Eggs are egg-shaped because the narrow end lets them roll in a circle rather than away off a cliff ledge.
Things that are spherical.Coin: A coin is a flat cylinder, and the only round part is its edge.
Things that are spherical.Pizza: Pizza dough is a flat disc, which is round but not spherical.
Things that are spherical.Frisbee: A Frisbee flies because it is a flat disc spinning like a wing, which would not work as a sphere.
Things that are spherical.Dice: Standard dice are cubes, and the opposite faces of a die always add up to seven.
Things that are spherical.Pyramid: Pyramids have flat triangular faces, and the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Things that are spherical.Book: Books are rectangular, and the oldest codex form came from stacking wax tablets.
Things that are spherical.Brick: Bricks are rectangular blocks, which is what makes them stackable, one of the oldest building materials.
Things that are spherical.Pencil: Pencils are usually hexagonal rather than round so they don't roll off the desk.

Fuzzy things.Peach: The fuzz on a peach is made of tiny hairs that probably protect the fruit from insects and moisture loss.
Fuzzy things.Kiwi fruit: It's also called the Chinese gooseberry, and it was renamed after New Zealand's fuzzy brown kiwi bird.
Fuzzy things.Tennis ball: The felt coating is wool and nylon, and it slows the ball and helps it grip the air, and the felt wears off in play.
Fuzzy things.Bumblebee: A bumblebee's fuzz traps heat and collects pollen, and it lets the bee fly in cold weather.
Fuzzy things.Teddy bear: Teddy bears were named after Theodore Roosevelt in 1902, and early ones were stuffed with straw.
Fuzzy things.Pipe cleaner: Pipe cleaners are also called chenille stems, which is French for caterpillar, and they were first for cleaning tobacco pipes.
Fuzzy things.Chick: Baby chicks are covered in down, the soft insulating feathers that keep them warm before they grow real feathers.
Fuzzy things.Pom-pom: Pom-poms are fluffy balls of yarn, and they were used on French sailors' hats.
Fuzzy things.Duckling: Ducklings are covered in fluffy down, and it's waterproofed by oil within days of hatching.
Fuzzy things.Bunny: Baby rabbits are born hairless and blind, and their fur grows in within a couple of weeks.
Fuzzy things.Kitten: Kittens' soft fur is short and fine, and they are born with their eyes closed.
Fuzzy things.Lamb: A lamb's fleece is wool, which has a crimp that traps air for warmth.
Fuzzy things.Apple: Apples float because about a quarter of their volume is air, and their skin is smooth.
Fuzzy things.Grape: Grapes have smooth skin, often with a natural waxy bloom.
Fuzzy things.Banana: Bananas are smooth, and the plant is the world's largest herb.
Fuzzy things.Window glass: Window glass is smooth and clear, and it is a liquid-like solid that doesn't flow over centuries, which is a myth.
Fuzzy things.Marble: Marbles are smooth glass balls, and the toy has been around since ancient times.
Fuzzy things.Balloon: A balloon is smooth stretchy rubber, and latex is from the rubber tree.
Fuzzy things.Snake: Snakes are smooth and dry, not slimy, and they shed the skin in one piece.
Fuzzy things.Frog: Frogs have smooth, moist skin that they partly breathe through.
Fuzzy things.Goldfish: Goldfish are scaly and smooth, with a memory far better than the three-second myth.
Fuzzy things.Ice cube: Ice cubes are smooth, and clear ice comes from freezing water slowly from one direction.
Fuzzy things.Plum: Plums have smooth skin with a pale waxy bloom.
Fuzzy things.Nectarine: A nectarine is a peach without the fuzz, caused by a single gene, so it's smooth, not fuzzy.

Gases at room temperature.Oxygen: Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of air, and in liquid form it's pale blue.
Gases at room temperature.Helium: Helium was spotted in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 before anyone found it on Earth, and it's named for Helios.
Gases at room temperature.Nitrogen: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of air, but plants can't use it until bacteria convert it.
Gases at room temperature.Carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04 percent of the air, yet plants depend on it.
Gases at room temperature.Hydrogen: Hydrogen is the lightest element and the most abundant one in the universe.
Gases at room temperature.Neon: Neon glows red-orange in a tube; other sign colors come from different gases or from phosphor coatings.
Gases at room temperature.Methane: Natural gas is mostly methane, and cattle belches are a notable source of it.
Gases at room temperature.Argon: Argon is the third most abundant gas in the air, about 1 percent, and it's used to fill light bulbs.
Gases at room temperature.Chlorine: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas that was used as a weapon in World War I and disinfects pools today.
Gases at room temperature.Carbon monoxide: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, hence its nickname the silent killer.
Gases at room temperature.Propane: Propane is stored as a liquid under pressure and boils into gas at about minus 42 degrees Celsius.
Gases at room temperature.Radon: Radon is a radioactive gas seeping from uranium decay in rock, and a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
Gases at room temperature.Mercury: Mercury is the only metal that's liquid at room temperature, but it evaporates, and its vapor is toxic.
Gases at room temperature.Bromine: Bromine is one of just two elements that are liquid at room temperature, a fuming reddish-brown that smells awful.
Gases at room temperature.Water: Water is liquid at room temperature; the invisible gas in the air is water vapor.
Gases at room temperature.Gasoline: Gasoline is a liquid, but its vapors are what ignite, and they're heavier than air.
Gases at room temperature.Iodine: Iodine is a solid that turns directly into purple gas when warmed, which is called sublimation.
Gases at room temperature.Sulfur: Sulfur is a yellow solid that burns with a blue flame; the old word for it is brimstone.
Gases at room temperature.Gallium: Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so it can melt in your hand but is a solid at room temperature.
Gases at room temperature.Dry ice: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide that turns directly into gas at minus 78.5 degrees Celsius, but it's a solid, not a gas.
Gases at room temperature.Salt: Table salt is a crystalline solid that doesn't melt until about 800 degrees Celsius.
Gases at room temperature.Iron: Iron melts at about 1,538 degrees Celsius, far above room temperature.
Gases at room temperature.Candle wax: A candle burns vaporized wax, not the solid wax itself.
Gases at room temperature.Rubbing alcohol: Rubbing alcohol is liquid at room temperature but evaporates quickly, cooling your skin.

Things that grow back after being lost.Hair: Each strand grows about a centimeter a month, and a hair lost from a healthy follicle is replaced by a new one in the same spot.
Things that grow back after being lost.Fingernails: Fingernails grow about three millimeters a month, around three times faster than toenails, and a lost one regrows in roughly six months.
Things that grow back after being lost.Lizard tail: Many lizards drop their tails to escape predators, and the replacement is made of cartilage, not bone, and it looks different.
Things that grow back after being lost.Starfish arm: A sea star can regrow a lost arm, and some species can even regrow a full body from a single arm and a piece of its center.
Things that grow back after being lost.Mowed grass: Grass grows from the base of its blades, not the tip, which is why it survives mowing and grazing so well.
Things that grow back after being lost.Deer antlers: Deer shed their antlers each year, and regrow them in a few months, which makes them one of the fastest-growing tissues in any mammal.
Things that grow back after being lost.Shark teeth: A shark may go through tens of thousands of teeth in a lifetime, with new ones moving forward from rows behind.
Things that grow back after being lost.Axolotl limb: This Mexican salamander can regrow whole limbs, parts of the heart and even parts of its brain, so scientists study it for medicine.
Things that grow back after being lost.Sheep's wool: Sheep are shorn about once a year, and the fleece grows back, and some breeds have been bred to grow wool without stopping.
Things that grow back after being lost.Beard: A beard grows about half an inch a month, and shaved whiskers do not grow back thicker, despite the popular myth.
Things that grow back after being lost.Toenails: Toenails take 12 to 18 months to regrow fully, roughly three times longer than a lost fingernail.
Things that grow back after being lost.Human finger: A fingertip can regrow in young children if cut above the nail base, but a whole finger lost does not grow back.
Things that grow back after being lost.Adult human tooth: Humans get just two sets of teeth, and the second set is the last, so a lost adult tooth is gone for good.
Things that grow back after being lost.Human arm: Unlike salamanders, people can't regrow an arm, though the liver and skin can repair themselves surprisingly well.
Things that grow back after being lost.Human eye: The human eye cannot regrow when lost, though the cornea can heal from minor damage in days.
Things that grow back after being lost.Dog's leg: Mammals like dogs don't regenerate whole limbs, so a lost leg is gone permanently, although they adapt well to three legs.
Things that grow back after being lost.Human nose: The nose is mostly cartilage, which has very limited ability to repair itself, so it doesn't regrow if lost.
Things that grow back after being lost.Cat's tail: A cat's tail doesn't regrow when lost, unlike a lizard's, and it plays a key role in the cat's balance.
Things that grow back after being lost.Human ear: Ear cartilage can't regrow, but in 2022 surgeons implanted a lab-grown ear made from a patient's own cells.
Things that grow back after being lost.Bird wing: Birds can't regrow wings, though feathers regrow during molting, and a lost flight feather can be replaced within weeks.
Things that grow back after being lost.Horse's leg: A horse's leg cannot regrow once lost, and the long legs are one reason a leg injury is so serious for them.
Things that grow back after being lost.Human toe: A lost toe doesn't grow back, although a toenail will, and in small children a clean fingertip cut can sometimes regrow too.
Things that grow back after being lost.Kneecap: The kneecap, or patella, is the largest sesamoid bone in the body, and it will not regrow if removed.
Things that grow back after being lost.Elephant trunk: An elephant's trunk has about 40,000 muscles and tendons, and it cannot regrow, so a lost one is a serious threat to survival.

Fictional cars from TV and film.Hummer: A real civilian version of the military Humvee, so not a fictional car.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Jeep Wrangler: A real off-roader descended from WWII Jeeps, so it's not a fictional car.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Testarossa: A real Ferrari, famous for the Miami Vice TV show, but not a fictional car.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Fiat 500: A real Italian small car from 1957, so no fiction.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Land Rover: A real British off-roader dating to 1948, not a fictional car.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Tesla Model S: A real electric sedan launched in 2012, so not fictional.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Toyota Corolla: A real car, the best-selling nameplate of all time, so it's not fictional.
Fictional cars from TV and film.Chevy Impala: A real Chevrolet sold since 1958, so it's not fictional, though a black 1967 Impala is the famous car in the TV show Supernatural.

Types of bridge.Suspension: The deck hangs from cables strung between towers, and the Akashi Kaikyo in Japan has a central span of nearly two kilometres.
Types of bridge.Drawbridge: Castles used drawbridges to lift the bridge and block attackers, and Tower Bridge in London uses a similar principle.
Types of bridge.Arch: Romans perfected the stone arch, and many of their arched bridges still stand after nearly 2,000 years.
Types of bridge.Cantilever: Two arms reach out from supports and meet in the middle, and the Forth Bridge is the famous example.
Types of bridge.Truss: The bridge uses a triangle framework, which spreads loads efficiently, and it's very common for railways.
Types of bridge.Pontoon: It floats on hollow boats or barges, and military engineers often build quick pontoon bridges across rivers.
Types of bridge.Footbridge: A bridge meant only for pedestrians, and some are tiny, such as a plank across a stream.
Types of bridge.Viaduct: A long bridge with many spans, carrying a road or railway over a valley, with the Millau Viaduct the tallest in the world.
Types of bridge.Swing bridge: A swing bridge rotates horizontally on a central pier to let boats through, as at Tyne Bridge in Newcastle.
Types of bridge.Rope bridge: A bridge of ropes, such as the Inca bridge of woven grass that is still rebuilt each year in Peru.
Types of bridge.Cable-stayed: Cables run straight from towers to the deck, so unlike a suspension bridge, it doesn't need anchorages at both ends.
Types of bridge.Tunnel: It goes under, not over, so it isn't a bridge, though both cross obstacles.
Types of bridge.Lock: A lock raises or lowers boats between water levels, and isn't a bridge, though many canals have bridges beside.
Types of bridge.Dam: A dam blocks a river, so it doesn't carry traffic across, though many have roads on top.
Types of bridge.Levee: An embankment against floods, not a bridge.
Types of bridge.Pier: A pier juts out into the water, and a bridge spans a gap, so it is not one.
Types of bridge.Jetty: It protects a harbour or is a landing stage, and doesn't cross a gap.
Types of bridge.Dock: A place where ships moor, so it's a waterfront structure rather than a bridge, though many docks are crossed by small swing bridges.
Types of bridge.Roundabout: A road junction where traffic circles, not a bridge, though some roundabouts sit on top of one.
Types of bridge.Underpass: It's a road passing beneath another, so you could say it's the underside of a bridge, but it's not a type.
Types of bridge.Moat: A moat is a water-filled ditch, which castles crossed with bridges, but it isn't a bridge.
Types of bridge.Breakwater: A barrier protecting a harbour from waves, not a bridge.
Types of bridge.Ditch: A trench, which people cross with a bridge, so it is not a bridge itself.
Types of bridge.Cul-de-sac: French for 'bottom of the bag', it's a dead-end street, so no span.

Parts of a suit jacket.Lapel: A lapel's buttonhole was once meant for fastening the collar up against the cold, and now it usually holds a flower.
Parts of a suit jacket.Collar: The part around your neck comes in notched and peaked versions; the peaked style is typically the dressier of the two.
Parts of a suit jacket.Cuff: Real tailored jackets sometimes have working buttonholes on the sleeve, called surgeon's cuffs, which let doctors roll up their sleeves.
Parts of a suit jacket.Breast pocket: A pocket on the left chest is traditionally for a folded handkerchief and is not meant to hold anything heavy.
Parts of a suit jacket.Vent: Slits in the back hem, called vents, let you sit and reach into pockets without wrinkling the jacket; Americans often have one and Europeans two.
Parts of a suit jacket.Button: Traditional etiquette says that the bottom button on a suit jacket should be left open.
Parts of a suit jacket.Sleeve: Many jackets have four working buttons on each sleeve, and few men ever undo them.
Parts of a suit jacket.Lining: The inner layer is often silk or viscose and makes the jacket slide on easily, while hiding all the stitching and padding inside.
Parts of a suit jacket.Buttonhole: The small hole that a button passes through is hand-sewn on top-quality suits, which can take a tailor several minutes per hole.
Parts of a suit jacket.Shoulder pad: Padding at the shoulder gives the jacket structure, and the soft Italian style often skips it entirely.
Parts of a suit jacket.Sole: This is part of a shoe, and the sole is what meets the ground.
Parts of a suit jacket.Heel: The heel is the raised back of a shoe, not a jacket part.
Parts of a suit jacket.Tongue: A shoe's tongue sits under the laces to protect your foot, and a jacket lacks any equivalent.
Parts of a suit jacket.Eyelet: Eyelets are the lace holes in shoes, and a suit jacket has none.
Parts of a suit jacket.Aglet: The aglet is the small plastic or metal tip on a shoelace, and it has a name most people have never learned.
Parts of a suit jacket.Brim: A brim is the rim of a hat that shades the face.
Parts of a suit jacket.Waistband: The waistband belongs to trousers or skirts, and a jacket does not have one.
Parts of a suit jacket.Fly: A fly is the front opening on trousers, so it is on the lower half of a suit.
Parts of a suit jacket.Inseam: The inseam is the inner-leg seam of trousers, so it is on the lower half of a suit.
Parts of a suit jacket.Belt loop: Belt loops are on trousers, and a suit jacket does not have them.
Parts of a suit jacket.Toe cap: A toe cap is the reinforced front of a shoe, which is a trap since it sounds like an item of clothing.
Parts of a suit jacket.Insole: The insole is the layer inside a shoe against your foot, and is no part of a jacket.
Parts of a suit jacket.Visor: A visor is the peak on a cap or helmet, and not a jacket part.
Parts of a suit jacket.Hatband: A hatband wraps around the base of a hat's crown, and sits on a hat, not a jacket.

Holidays that fall in December.Christmas: December 25 was fixed for Christmas in the 4th century, close to the Roman winter solstice festivals.
Holidays that fall in December.Kwanzaa: Runs from December 26 to January 1, and was created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga as a celebration of African American heritage.
Holidays that fall in December.Boxing Day: December 26, when servants and tradespeople traditionally got gifts in boxes from their employers.
Holidays that fall in December.New Year's Eve: December 31, which is celebrated across the world, and Times Square's ball has dropped since 1907.
Holidays that fall in December.St. Nicholas Day: December 6, when children in many European countries find treats in their shoes or stockings.
Holidays that fall in December.St. Lucia Day: December 13, when girls in Sweden wear candle crowns and carry saffron buns in a procession.
Holidays that fall in December.Christmas Eve: December 24, when many countries open gifts or hold the main feast.
Holidays that fall in December.Hogmanay: Scotland's New Year celebration, with first-footing, a custom in which the first visitor brings luck.
Holidays that fall in December.Las Posadas: Nine nights from December 16 in Mexico, re-enacting Mary and Joseph's search for lodging with processions and piñatas.
Holidays that fall in December.Saturnalia: An ancient Roman festival around December 17, with gift-giving and a role-reversal in which slaves were served.
Holidays that fall in December.Easter: Easter moves each spring, set by the full moon after the spring equinox, so it never falls in December.
Holidays that fall in December.Halloween: Halloween falls on October 31, a night tied to the Celtic festival of Samhain.
Holidays that fall in December.Valentine's Day: Valentine's Day is always February 14, and it is tied to a saint named Valentine.
Holidays that fall in December.Diwali: Diwali moves with the lunar calendar and falls in October or November, so it just misses December.
Holidays that fall in December.St. Patrick's Day: St. Patrick's Day is March 17, honoring Ireland's patron saint.
Holidays that fall in December.Mardi Gras: Mardi Gras is the day before Lent begins, so it moves each year with Easter and falls in winter or early spring.
Holidays that fall in December.Groundhog Day: Groundhog Day is February 2, when a groundhog supposedly forecasts the weather.
Holidays that fall in December.Bastille Day: Bastille Day is July 14, French national day, marking the storming of the Bastille in 1789.
Holidays that fall in December.Cinco de Mayo: Cinco de Mayo is May 5 and marks the 1862 Battle of Puebla, not Mexican independence.
Holidays that fall in December.Guy Fawkes Night: Guy Fawkes Night is November 5, remembering the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, and it falls a month before December.
Holidays that fall in December.Labor Day: Labor Day is the first Monday of September in the US, honoring workers.
Holidays that fall in December.Holi: Holi is a spring festival of colors, on the full moon in March, so it's not in December.
Holidays that fall in December.Canada Day: Canada Day is July 1, marking the 1867 confederation of Canada, so it falls in summer.
Holidays that fall in December.Midsummer: Midsummer falls around June 21 to 24, near the summer solstice, so it's the opposite of December.

Types of dress.Sundress: It is made for warm weather, with straps or bare shoulders, and its name goes back to the 1800s.
Types of dress.Maxi dress: Floor-length maxi dresses took off in the late 1960s, as an answer to the micro-miniskirt.
Types of dress.Shift dress: Straight and waistless, the shift dress rose in the 1960s and was worn by Jackie Kennedy.
Types of dress.Ball gown: A ball gown is a floor-length formal dress with a full skirt, made for the most formal dances.
Types of dress.Wrap dress: Diane von Furstenberg's 1974 design made the wrap dress an icon, a dress you could tie in seconds.
Types of dress.Slip dress: Borrowed from lingerie, the slip dress hit the mainstream in the 1990s when Kate Moss wore one.
Types of dress.Cocktail dress: The cocktail dress appeared in the 1920s as cocktail parties became popular during Prohibition.
Types of dress.Shirtdress: As the name says, it is cut like a men's shirt, with a collar and buttons, but is a dress.
Types of dress.Pinafore: Pinafore means pinned afore, since it was an apron pinned on the front, and it became a dress.
Types of dress.Little black dress: Coco Chanel made it famous in 1926; Vogue compared it to the Model T Ford, saying it would become a uniform.
Types of dress.Prom dress: Prom comes from promenade, a stroll that opened formal dances, and the dress is an American tradition.
Types of dress.Blazer: A blazer is a jacket, and the name may come from the red jackets of a boat club, though that is debated.
Types of dress.Jumpsuit: It joins top and trousers into one garment, so a jumpsuit is not a dress.
Types of dress.Romper: A romper is a one-piece with shorts, originally designed for children, which is not a dress.
Types of dress.Kilt: The kilt is a pleated tartan garment wrapped around the waist, more a skirt than a dress.
Types of dress.Tutu: Short, stiff and made of layers of net, the tutu is a skirt and never a full dress.
Types of dress.Blouse: A blouse only covers the top, so it can't be a dress.
Types of dress.Pantsuit: A pantsuit has trousers, which makes it not a dress, and it became a political symbol in the 1990s.
Types of dress.Overalls: Overalls are bibbed trousers, and the pinafore is the dress cousin of them.
Types of dress.Leotard: The leotard was named for French trapeze artist Jules Leotard, and it is a one-piece bodysuit.
Types of dress.Poncho: Poncho comes from the Andes, and it is a single blanket with a hole for the head.
Types of dress.Sarong: Wrapped around the waist, the sarong takes its name from a Malay word meaning to sheathe.
Types of dress.Tracksuit: A tracksuit is for exercise, and tracksuits came to fashion in the 1970s.
Types of dress.Cardigan: The cardigan is named after the 7th Earl of Cardigan, a commander in the Crimean War.
